fullPassage: When we think about science, we might consider it as a domain reserved exclusively for scientists in long, white lab coats who spend their days conducting experiments and analyzing data. They seem to have very little in common with ordinary people like us. However, this perception is far from the truth. In reality, science belongs to everyone, and we all have the ability to play a role in the advancement of science. There have been numerous citizen science projects in which ordinary people have made contributions to remarkable scientific accomplishments. Let’s take a look at two of them. Classifying Galaxies Kevin Schawinski was a young astronomy researcher studying black holes and the evolution of galaxies at the University of Oxford. This might sound exciting, but his job there was dull and time-consuming. He had to classify around one million images of galaxies according to their shape. Since they all looked similar but were actually shaped slightly differently, the best way to do this was to sort them while looking at each one individually. Of course, this would require a tremendous amount of time. It took Schawinski a whole week to classify just 50,000 galaxies. He thought, “But what about the remaining 950,000?” One evening after work, Schawinski met a friend named Chris Lintott and complained about the situation. Lintott suggested that he turn to the Internet to ask other people for help. Eventually, the two men ended up launching a crowdsourced online project known as Galaxy Zoo. The website was kept as simple as possible, with a very basic design and an easy-to-use interface. This allowed those who wanted to participate to get started quickly. New visitors were greeted with a brief tutorial that explained the project. Then they were shown an image of a galaxy and asked to click buttons that described its features. Is the galaxy smooth and rounded? Is its shape an oval or a spiral? After completion of the tutorial and a little bit of practice, the participants were able to classify galaxies effectively. It was online media that helped spread the word about Galaxy Zoo, bringing more and more participants to the website. Shortly after the website was launched, nearly 70,000 classifications were being made per hour. In a year and a half, more than 80,000 individuals participated, and they made more than 75 million classifications. If it had not been for those participants, Schawinski couldn’t have classified that many images. In fact, it would have taken him decades on his own. More than 15 years have passed since the project first began in 2007. Galaxy Zoo has now grown into Zooniverse, which is one of the most popular platforms on the Internet for ordinary people who want to participate in science projects. It is more active than ever before, with about 2 million registered users worldwide. It now offers a wide range of projects in astronomy, biology, physics, and more. If you want to get involved, you should definitely check it out! Chasing Steve In Alberta, Canada, there were some “aurora chasers” who formed an informal group online. They would leave their homes at night and try to get exceptional photographs of auroras. Then they would share them with the rest of the group. In the summer of 2014, the group members began to notice something strange appearing in the night sky. There were unusual ribbons of green and purple light, some of which seemed to stretch for thousands of kilometers. Sometimes they lasted for just a few minutes, while other times they remained in the sky for a whole hour. They were similar in appearance to auroras, yet they possessed some notably different features. Unsure of what they were, the group decided to name the phenomenon “Steve,” based on a scene from an animated movie where some characters give that name to an unfamiliar object. After photographing Steve for several years and discussing what it might be, the group members decided to get help from experts. They showed their photos of Steve to a professor of astronomy at a local university and a scientist at NASA. Surprisingly, neither of them had any idea what Steve was. They confirmed that it was not an aurora, but it did not resemble anything they had seen before. They realized that the group had discovered a new type of phenomenon that had never been properly studied. In order to learn more about it, NASA funded a citizen science project involving the public. The project asked ordinary people to gather photos of Steve and send them to NASA. It is still in progress today. In honor of the aurora chasers who first discovered the phenomenon, the name “Steve” has been kept. However, it is now written in all capital letters and stands for “Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement.” Experts have acknowledged that it is the dedicated members of the aurora chasers group that deserve the credit for discovering STEVE. If it had not been for them, it might have remained unnoticed forever. There are many interesting theories about STEVE, but none of them have been proven for certain. Scientists and citizens continue to collaborate to solve this mystery, and they are learning more and more about STEVE every day. Most of the individuals involved in these two projects are not professional scientists. Instead, they are citizen scientists — ordinary people who desire to help advance science in areas that they are interested in. Even though citizen scientists may not have science degrees or long, white lab coats, they are still capable of making valuable contributions to science. You can become one as well if you have curiosity and an interest in taking part in scientific research. The next great scientific achievement could be made by citizen scientists volunteering their time for the purpose of better understanding the world.

웹사이트가 개설된 직후 시간당 약 7,000건의 분류가 이뤄졌다.
현재 Zooniverse의 등록 사용자는 약 20만 명이다.

questions.passage: The aurora chasers, who ①<u>spent</u> many nights outdoors, took countless photos of the mysterious lights. They showed the images to several experts, none of ②<u>whom</u> could explain the phenomenon. The scientists confirmed that it was not an aurora, but it did not ③<u>resemble</u> anything they had seen before. Realizing that they ④<u>discovering</u> a completely new type of phenomenon, the researchers asked the public to send more photos.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.korean: ④ discovering → had discovered: 분사구문 안에서도 목적어를 취하는 정동사가 필요하므로 had discovered
det.analysis:
✅ ① spent: 'who spent many nights outdoors'에서 관계사절의 과거 시제 정동사로 적절
✅ ② whom: 'none of whom could explain'에서 전치사 of의 목적어 역할을 하는 목적격 관계대명사로 적절
✅ ③ resemble: 'it did not resemble anything'에서 조동사 did 뒤 동사원형으로 적절
❌ ④ discovering → had discovered: 'Realizing that they ___ a completely new type of phenomenon'에서 that절의 주어(they) 뒤에는 정동사가 필요하다. discovering(현재분사)은 정동사가 될 수 없으므로, 앞선 시점을 나타내는 had discovered로 고쳐야 한다 ← 정답
det.tip: that절 안에도 주어(they)에 맞는 정동사가 필요합니다: they had discovered

questions.passage: Shortly after the website was launched, nearly 70,000 classifications were being made per hour.  In a year and a half, more than 80,000 individuals participated, and they made more than 75 million classifications.  If it had not been for those participants, Schawinski couldn’t have classified that many images.  In fact, it would have taken him decades on his own.
questions.stem: 위 글에 따르면, Schawinski가 혼자서 100만 개의 은하를 분류했다면 걸렸을 것이라고 언급한 기간을 나타내는 단어를 본문에서 찾아 쓰시오. (1단어, 영어로)

det.analysis: 본문 'In fact, it would have taken him decades on his own.'에서 참여자들이 없었다면, 즉 혼자서 그 많은 은하를 분류했다면 '수십 년(decades)'이 걸렸을 것이라고 밝혔다.
det.tip: it would have taken him decades on his own(혼자서는 수십 년이 걸렸을 것)에서 decades를 찾습니다.

questions.passage: In honor of the aurora chasers who first discovered the phenomenon, the name “Steve” has been kept.  However, it is now written in all capital letters and stands for “Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement. ” Experts have acknowledged that it is the dedicated members of the aurora chasers group that deserve the credit for discovering STEVE.
questions.stem: 위 글에 따르면, 대문자 STEVE는 'Strong Thermal Emission Velocity'에 이어지는 한 단어까지 포함한 명칭의 약자이다. 그 마지막 한 단어를 본문에서 찾아 쓰시오. (1단어, 영어로)

det.analysis: 본문 'it is now written in all capital letters and stands for "Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement."'에서 대문자 STEVE는 'Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement'의 약자다. 마지막 단어는 Enhancement(증대)이다.
det.tip: Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement에서 마지막 단어 Enhancement를 찾습니다.

questions.passage: The next great scientific achievement could be made by citizen scientists __________ (volunteer) their time for the purpose of better understanding the world.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 흐름에 맞도록 괄호 안에 주어진 단어를 알맞은 형태로 바꿔 쓰시오. (1단어, 영어로)

det.analysis: 구문 분석: 'citizen scientists ___ their time'에서 빈칸 뒤에 목적어(their time)가 있고, 앞의 명사 citizen scientists(자신의 시간을 자발적으로 내는 시민 과학자들)를 능동으로 꾸며 준다. 따라서 동사원형 volunteer를 현재분사 volunteering(자발적으로 ~하는)으로 바꿔야 한다.
det.tip: 명사를 능동으로 꾸미는 현재분사(-ing): scientists volunteering their time(시간을 자발적으로 내는 과학자들)

questions.passage: When we think about science, we might consider it as a domain reserved exclusively for scientists in long, white lab coats who spend their days conducting experiments and analyzing data.  They seem to have very little in common with ordinary people like us.  However, this perception is far from the truth.  In reality, science belongs to everyone, and we all have the ability to play a role in the advancement of science.  There have been numerous citizen science projects in which ordinary people have made contributions to remarkable scientific accomplishments.  Let’s take a look at two of them.  Classifying Galaxies Kevin Schawinski was a young astronomy researcher studying black holes and the evolution of galaxies at the University of Oxford.  This might sound exciting, but his job there was dull and time-consuming.
questions.stem: 위 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① 대학·NASA의 협력은 일부 사례일 뿐 전체 주제가 아님
❌ ② 웹사이트 설계법은 Galaxy Zoo 사례의 세부 내용일 뿐임
✅ ③ Galaxy Zoo와 STEVE 사례를 통해 '평범한 사람들도 시민 과학으로 과학 발전에 기여할 수 있다'는 것이 글 전체의 주제 ← 정답
❌ ④ 오로라와 STEVE의 차이는 두 번째 사례의 일부일 뿐 전체 주제가 아님
det.tip: 두 사례(Galaxy Zoo, STEVE)를 관통하는 것은 '시민 과학자의 기여'입니다.

ch: 천문학 연구는 반드시 대학과 NASA의 협력을 통해서만 가능하다
인터넷 웹사이트를 쉽고 간단하게 설계하는 다양한 방법
평범한 사람들도 시민 과학을 통해 과학 발전에 의미 있게 기여할 수 있다
오로라와 STEVE의 과학적 차이를 밝히려는 최신 연구 동향

This might sound exciting, but his job there was dull and time-consuming.
questions.stem: 위 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① 본문 'You can become one as well if you have curiosity and an interest in taking part in scientific research'와 통하는 핵심 메시지 ← 정답
❌ ② 글은 오히려 '과학은 모두의 것'이라고 하므로 요지와 반대
❌ ③ 학위가 없어도 기여할 수 있다고 했으므로 반대
❌ ④ 시민 과학이 실제로 remarkable accomplishments(놀라운 성과)에 기여했다고 했으므로 반대
det.tip: curiosity와 interest만 있으면 누구나 시민 과학자가 될 수 있다는 것이 요지입니다.

ch: 호기심과 참여 의지가 있다면 누구나 시민 과학자가 되어 과학에 기여할 수 있다
과학은 흰 가운을 입은 전문가만의 영역이라 일반인은 접근하기 어렵다
위대한 과학적 업적은 오직 오랜 학위 과정을 거친 사람만이 이룰 수 있다
시민 과학 프로젝트는 재미는 있으나 실제 과학 발전에는 도움이 되지 않는다

questions.passage: Most of the individuals involved in these two projects are not professional scientists.  Instead, they are citizen scientists — ordinary people who desire to help advance science in areas that they are interested in.  Even though citizen scientists may not have science degrees or long, white lab coats, __________.  You can become one as well if you have curiosity and an interest in taking part in scientific research.
questions.stem:
위 글의 내용을 바탕으로, 다음 우리말에 맞도록 주어진 조건에 따라 영작하시오. (영어로)

'그들은 여전히 과학에 가치 있는 기여를 할 수 있다.'

[조건]
(1) are, capable, contributions, making, of, science, still, they, to, valuable를 모두 사용할 것
(2) 정확히 10단어로 쓸 것

det.korean: they are still capable of making valuable contributions to science
det.analysis:
구문 분석:
- they(주어) + are(동사) + still(부사): 그들은 여전히
- be capable of + 동명사(-ing): '~할 수 있다'라는 표현이므로 capable of making(만들 수 있는)
- valuable contributions(가치 있는 기여)가 making의 목적어
- to science(과학에)로 마무리
- 순서대로 놓으면 they / are / still / capable / of / making / valuable / contributions / to / science
det.tip: be capable of + 동명사(-ing): ~할 수 있다 / make a contribution to ~ (~에 기여하다)
